grammarPoints.title: Adverbs of frequency
grammarPoints.summary: Adverbs of frequency like 'always' and 'never' tell us how often something happens and usually go before the main verb or after the verb 'be'.
grammarPoints.explanation:
Adverbs of frequency like *always*, *usually*, *often*, *sometimes*, and *never* tell us how frequently an action happens. They help us describe routines and habits.

These adverbs usually go *before* the main verb in a sentence. For example: "I *always* drink coffee in the morning." "She *never* eats meat."

If the verb is "be" (am, is, are), the adverb of frequency usually goes *after* the "be" verb. For example: "He *is usually* happy." "They *are often* late."

The adverb "sometimes" can also go at the beginning or end of a sentence for emphasis, but the most common placement is before the main verb.
patterns: Subject + adverb of frequency + main verb

examples.text: I *always* eat breakfast before work.
examples.note: The adverb 'always' comes before the main verb 'eat'.

examples.text: She *is usually* on time for meetings.
examples.note: The adverb 'usually' comes after the 'be' verb 'is'.

examples.text: We *often* visit our grandparents on weekends.
examples.note: The adverb 'often' comes before the main verb 'visit'.

examples.text: *Sometimes* they go for a walk in the park.
examples.note: The adverb 'sometimes' is at the beginning for emphasis.

examples.text: He *never* forgets his keys.
examples.note: The adverb 'never' comes before the main verb 'forgets'.

examples.text: I usually have dinner at seven.
He is always full of ideas.

commonErrors.note: Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb.
Adverbs of frequency go after the 'be' verb.
Adverbs of frequency usually go before the main verb, not at the beginning.

grammarPoints.title: Adverbs of manner
grammarPoints.summary: Adverbs of manner like 'quickly', 'well', and 'hard' tell us *how* an action is done. They describe verbs.
grammarPoints.explanation:
Adverbs of manner describe *how* an action happens. They usually come after the verb they describe. For example, if someone runs, an adverb of manner can tell us *how* they run: 'They run *quickly*.'

Many adverbs of manner are formed by adding '-ly' to an adjective (e.g., 'quick' becomes 'quickly', 'careful' becomes 'carefully').

Some adverbs of manner are irregular. For example, the adverb form of 'good' is 'well'. The word 'hard' is both an adjective and an adverb, so it doesn't change (e.g., 'a hard worker' and 'work hard').

examples.text: She sings beautifully.
examples.note: Describes *how* she sings.

examples.text: He drives carefully on busy roads.
examples.note: Describes *how* he drives.

examples.text: They worked hard to finish the project.
examples.note: Describes *how* they worked.

examples.text: My brother speaks English very well.
examples.note: Describes *how* he speaks English.

examples.text: The children played happily in the park.
examples.note: Describes *how* the children played.

examples.text: "Why are you studying English so hard?" "To be an English teacher."
Mary spoke Japanese slowly.

commonErrors.note: Use 'well' (adverb) to describe a verb, not 'good' (adjective).
Add '-ly' to most adjectives to form adverbs of manner.
'Hard' is already an adverb; 'hardly' has a different meaning.

grammarPoints.title: And, but, or, because, so
grammarPoints.summary: Learn to connect two simple ideas or sentences into one longer sentence using 'and', 'but', 'or', 'because', and 'so'.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We often want to join two short sentences or ideas together to make one longer, more complete sentence. We use linking words like *and*, *but*, *or*, *because*, and *so* to do this. These words help show the relationship between the two ideas.

*And* adds more information. It connects two similar ideas or things. *But* shows a contrast or something unexpected. It connects two ideas that are different or opposite. *Or* gives a choice between two options.

*Because* tells us the reason for something. It answers the question "Why?". *So* tells us the result or consequence of something. It answers the question "What happened next?" or "What was the effect?".

examples.text: I like to read books, and I enjoy watching movies.
examples.note: 'And' adds a similar idea.

examples.text: It was sunny, but it was still cold outside.
examples.note: 'But' shows a contrast between the two ideas.

examples.text: Do you want to eat pizza, or would you prefer pasta?
examples.note: 'Or' offers a choice between two options.

examples.text: She was happy because she got a new job.
examples.note: 'Because' gives the reason for her happiness.

examples.text: He studied hard, so he passed the exam easily.
examples.note: 'So' shows the result of studying hard.

examples.text: Hurry up, or you'll be late.
I was going to write to you, but I was too busy.

commonErrors.wrong: I was tired, so I went to bed early because I was tired.
commonErrors.right: I was tired, so I went to bed early.
commonErrors.note: Avoid repeating the reason when using 'so'.

commonErrors.wrong: She likes apples, but she likes oranges.
commonErrors.right: She likes apples, and she likes oranges.
commonErrors.note: Use 'and' to connect two similar positive ideas.

commonErrors.wrong: He didn't come because he was sick.
commonErrors.right: He didn't come, because he was sick.
commonErrors.note: Remember to use a comma before 'because' when it connects two independent clauses.

grammarPoints.title: Comparative adjectives
grammarPoints.summary: Learn to compare two things using adjectives like 'taller', 'more interesting', 'better', and 'worse'.
grammarPoints.explanation:
When you want to compare two people, places, or things, you use *comparative adjectives*. These adjectives show which item has more of a certain quality than the other.

For most short adjectives (one or two syllables), you add *-er* to the end. For example, 'tall' becomes 'taller', and 'fast' becomes 'faster'. If the adjective ends in 'y', change 'y' to 'i' before adding '-er' (e.g., 'happy' becomes 'happier').

For longer adjectives (usually two or more syllables), you use the word *more* before the adjective. For example, 'beautiful' becomes 'more beautiful', and 'expensive' becomes 'more expensive'. After the comparative adjective, we often use *than* to introduce the second item in the comparison.

Some common adjectives have irregular comparative forms. 'Good' becomes *better*, and 'bad' becomes *worse*. Remember these special forms when you are comparing.

examples.text: My new apartment is *bigger* than my old one.
examples.note: Uses '-er' for a short adjective to compare two apartments.

examples.text: This book is *more interesting* than the movie.
examples.note: Uses 'more' for a longer adjective to compare a book and a movie.

examples.text: Today's weather is *better* than yesterday's.
examples.note: Uses the irregular comparative form of 'good'.

examples.text: The traffic was *worse* than I expected.
examples.note: Uses the irregular comparative form of 'bad'.

examples.text: She runs *faster* than her brother.
examples.note: Uses '-er' and 'than' to compare two people's running speed.

examples.text: This hotel is better than that other one.
My camera is better than yours.

commonErrors.wrong: This car is more faster than that one.
commonErrors.right: This car is *faster* than that one.
commonErrors.note: Do not use 'more' with adjectives that already have '-er'.
Always use 'than' after a comparative adjective when comparing two things.
Use the irregular form 'better' for 'good'.

grammarPoints.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
grammarPoints.summary: Learn to use 'a', 'an', and plural forms correctly with nouns you can count (countable) and nouns you cannot count (uncountable).
grammarPoints.explanation:
Nouns are words for people, places, things, or ideas. In English, nouns can be *countable* or *uncountable*. Knowing the difference helps you use them correctly with 'a', 'an', 'some', and plural forms.

*Countable nouns* are things you can count. They have both a singular form (one) and a plural form (more than one). For example, 'apple' is singular, 'apples' is plural. You can use 'a' or 'an' with singular countable nouns: 'a book', 'an orange'.

*Uncountable nouns* are things you cannot count individually. These often include liquids, abstract ideas, or materials. For example, 'water', 'information', 'music'. They usually don't have a plural form and you don't use 'a' or 'an' directly before them. Instead, you might use words like 'some' or 'a lot of'.

examples.text: I need *a new pen* for my class.
examples.note: 'Pen' is a singular countable noun, so we use 'a'.

examples.text: She bought *three apples* at the market.
examples.note: 'Apples' is a plural countable noun, so we use a number.

examples.text: Can I have *some water*, please?
examples.note: 'Water' is an uncountable noun, so we use 'some' instead of 'a/an'.

examples.text: There are *many chairs* in the meeting room.
examples.note: 'Chairs' is a plural countable noun, so we use 'many'.

examples.text: He always listens to *music* when he works.
examples.note: 'Music' is an uncountable noun; it doesn't take 'a/an' or a plural form here.

examples.text: I want some money.
My brother has many more good books than I do.

commonErrors.note: 'Advice' is an uncountable noun, so we use 'some'.

commonErrors.right: She has a lot of information.
commonErrors.note: 'Information' is an uncountable noun and does not have a plural form.
'Water' is an uncountable noun, so we use 'some' or 'a glass of'.

grammarPoints.title: Going to
grammarPoints.summary: Use "going to" to talk about future plans you have already made or to make predictions based on what you see now.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use *going to* to talk about future plans that you have already decided. These are not sudden decisions, but things you have thought about and planned.

We also use *going to* to make predictions about the future when we have clear evidence in the present. This means you can see or hear something now that tells you what will happen.
patterns: Subject + be (am/is/are) + going to + base verb
Subject + be (am/is/are) + not + going to + base verb
Be (Am/Is/Are) + Subject + going to + base verb?

examples.text: I'm going to start a new hobby next month.
examples.note: This shows a plan that has already been decided.

examples.text: Look at those dark clouds! It's going to rain soon.
examples.note: This is a prediction based on current evidence (dark clouds).

examples.text: They are going to visit their grandparents this summer.
examples.note: This describes a future plan they have made.

examples.text: Be careful! You're going to drop that plate.
examples.note: This is a prediction based on what is happening right now.

examples.text: She isn't going to come to the party tonight.
examples.note: This is a negative statement about a future plan.

examples.text: This afternoon the weather is going to get worse.
I am going to Hawaii next year.

commonErrors.wrong: He going to call me later.
commonErrors.right: He *is* going to call me later.
commonErrors.note: Remember to use the correct form of 'be' (am/is/are) before 'going to'.

commonErrors.wrong: We are going buy a new TV.
commonErrors.right: We are going *to* buy a new TV.
commonErrors.note: Always include 'to' after 'going' and before the base verb.
Make sure the 'be' verb agrees with the subject (e.g., 'they are', 'he is').

grammarPoints.title: Have to and must
grammarPoints.summary: Learn to use "have to" and "must" to talk about things that are necessary or rules you need to follow.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use *have to* and *must* to say that something is necessary or that there is an obligation. Both can be used for rules.

*Must* often shows a strong personal feeling of obligation or a rule that comes directly from the speaker. For example, "I *must* remember her birthday" shows a personal decision. *Have to* often shows an obligation that comes from outside, like a rule or a schedule. For example, "I *have to* wear a uniform at work" is an external rule.

For negative sentences, there is a big difference. *Don't have to* means something is *not necessary*. For example, "You *don't have to* come if you're busy." *Must not* means something is *forbidden* or not allowed. For example, "You *must not* touch the art." This is a strong prohibition.
patterns: Subject + don't/doesn't have to + base verb

examples.text: You must finish your homework before watching TV.
examples.note: Shows a strong obligation, perhaps from a parent or teacher.

examples.text: I have to go to the dentist tomorrow morning.
examples.note: Shows an external obligation due to an appointment.

examples.text: She doesn't have to work on Saturdays.
examples.note: Indicates that working on Saturdays is not necessary for her.

examples.text: Visitors must not feed the animals at the zoo.
examples.note: Shows a strong rule or prohibition.

examples.text: We have to buy tickets for the concert soon.
examples.note: Shows an external necessity to get tickets before they sell out.

examples.text: We must think about friends.
I have to do my homework.

commonErrors.note: Do not use 'to' after 'must'.

commonErrors.wrong: He don't have to leave yet.
commonErrors.right: He doesn't have to leave yet.
commonErrors.note: Use 'doesn't' with 'he/she/it' for 'have to'.

commonErrors.wrong: You must not to talk during the exam.
commonErrors.right: You must not talk during the exam.
commonErrors.note: Do not use 'to' after 'must not'.

grammarPoints.title: Imperatives
grammarPoints.summary: Imperatives tell someone to do something. We use them for instructions, warnings, and invitations, and 'don't' for negative commands.
grammarPoints.explanation:
Imperatives are verbs that give a direct command, instruction, warning, or invitation. They tell someone what to do or not to do. We use the base form of the verb for positive imperatives.

For example, if you want someone to open a book, you say, "Open the book." If you want to invite someone to sit, you say, "Have a seat."

To make an imperative negative, we use *don't* before the base form of the verb. For example, "Don't touch that!" is a warning not to touch something. We usually don't use a subject with imperatives because it's clear who you are talking to.

examples.text: Turn left at the next traffic light.
examples.note: This is an instruction for giving directions.

examples.text: Don't forget your umbrella today.
examples.note: This is a warning or a reminder.

examples.text: Come in and make yourself comfortable.
examples.note: This is an invitation.

examples.text: Be careful when you cross the street.
examples.note: This is a warning.

examples.text: Please wait here for a moment.
examples.note: This is a polite instruction or request.

examples.text: Hurry up. You'll be late for school.

commonErrors.note: Do not use a subject with imperatives.
Use 'don't' for negative imperatives.
Use the base form of the verb, not the infinitive.

grammarPoints.title: Like, love and hate + -ing
grammarPoints.summary: Use 'like', 'love', and 'hate' followed by a verb ending in '-ing' to talk about things you enjoy or dislike doing.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use verbs like *like*, *love*, and *hate* to express our feelings about activities. When we want to say what activity we like, love, or hate, we follow these verbs with another verb that ends in *-ing*.

For example, if you enjoy reading, you say "I like *reading*". If you really enjoy cooking, you say "She loves *cooking*". If you really dislike waiting, you say "They hate *waiting*".

Remember to use the correct form of 'like', 'love', or 'hate' (e.g., 'likes' for 'he/she/it') and always add '-ing' to the second verb.

examples.text: I like listening to music in the evenings.
examples.note: Shows a general enjoyment of an activity.

examples.text: My brother loves playing video games.
examples.note: Expresses strong enjoyment for an activity.

examples.text: We hate waiting in long lines at the store.
examples.note: Indicates a strong dislike for an activity.

examples.text: She doesn't like waking up early on weekends.
examples.note: Shows a mild dislike for an activity in the negative form.

examples.text: Do you like traveling to new places?
examples.note: Asks about someone's enjoyment of an activity.

examples.text: Tom doesn't like washing dishes.
Tom doesn't like doing homework.

commonErrors.note: Remember to use the -ing form after 'like' for general activities.
The second verb needs to end in -ing.
Don't forget the -s for 'he/she/it' with 'hate'.

grammarPoints.title: Much, many and a lot of
grammarPoints.summary: Learn to use 'much', 'many', and 'a lot of' to talk about quantities of things, distinguishing between countable and uncountable nouns.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use *much*, *many*, and *a lot of* to talk about quantities. The choice depends on whether the noun is *countable* or *uncountable*.

Use *many* with *countable nouns* (things you can count, like 'apples', 'friends'). Use *much* with *uncountable nouns* (things you can't count individually, like 'water', 'information'). We often use *much* and *many* in questions and negative sentences.

*A lot of* can be used with *both countable and uncountable nouns*. It's very common in positive sentences, but you can also use it in questions and negatives. *Lots of* means the same thing and is also very common.
patterns: a lot of + plural countable noun

examples.text: Do you have much time today?
examples.note: Uses 'much' with the uncountable noun 'time' in a question.

examples.text: There aren't many chairs in the room.
examples.note: Uses 'many' with the plural countable noun 'chairs' in a negative sentence.

examples.text: We have a lot of work to do this week.
examples.note: Uses 'a lot of' with the uncountable noun 'work' in a positive sentence.

examples.text: She bought a lot of new clothes for her trip.
examples.note: Uses 'a lot of' with the plural countable noun 'clothes' in a positive sentence.

examples.text: I don't drink much coffee in the evenings.
examples.note: Uses 'much' with the uncountable noun 'coffee' in a negative sentence.

examples.text: I think that there are many places to see there.
With your children away, you must have a lot of free time.

commonErrors.note: 'Friends' is countable, so use 'many'.
'Sugar' is uncountable, so use 'much'.

commonErrors.right: They have a lot of problems.
commonErrors.note: Always use 'of' after 'a lot' when it comes before a noun.

grammarPoints.title: Past continuous
grammarPoints.summary: Use the past continuous to talk about actions that were happening at a specific time in the past, often interrupted or happening at the same time as another action.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use the *past continuous* to describe actions that were in progress at a particular moment in the past. It focuses on the duration of an action, not its completion. Think of it as a snapshot of an ongoing activity.

The form of the past continuous is *was* or *were* + the *verb-ing* (present participle). We use 'was' for singular subjects (I, he, she, it) and 'were' for plural subjects (you, we, they).

We often use the past continuous with *when* to show that one action interrupted another. For example, "I was sleeping *when* the phone rang." We use *while* to show two actions happening at the same time. For example, "*While* I was cooking, my brother was watching TV."

examples.text: At 8 PM last night, I was eating dinner.
examples.note: Describes an action in progress at a specific past time.

examples.text: She was reading a book when her friend called.
examples.note: Shows an ongoing action interrupted by another past action.

examples.text: While they were walking, it started to rain.
examples.note: Connects two actions, one ongoing, one starting.

examples.text: He wasn't listening to the teacher.
examples.note: Negative form, showing an action was not in progress.

examples.text: Were you working on your project all afternoon?
examples.note: Question form, asking about an ongoing past action.

examples.text: Tom was walking slowly with his head down.
When I came home, he was cooking dinner.

commonErrors.wrong: I walked to the store when I saw my friend.
commonErrors.right: I was walking to the store when I saw my friend.
commonErrors.note: Use past continuous for the ongoing action that was interrupted.
Use 'were' for plural subjects.
Remember to add '-ing' to the main verb.

grammarPoints.title: Past simple: irregular verbs
grammarPoints.summary: Learn how to use common irregular verbs in the past simple to talk about finished actions and events.
grammarPoints.explanation:
In English, most verbs form the past simple by adding '-ed' (e.g., 'walk' becomes 'walked'). However, many common verbs are *irregular*.

Irregular verbs do not follow this rule. Instead, they change their form in different ways (e.g., 'go' becomes 'went', 'eat' becomes 'ate'). You need to learn these forms by heart.

We use the past simple for actions that started and finished at a specific time in the past.

examples.text: I *went* to the market this morning.
examples.note: Describes a completed action in the past.

examples.text: She *ate* a delicious meal last night.
examples.note: Shows a finished event at a specific past time.

examples.text: They *had* a lot of fun on their trip.
examples.note: Talks about a past experience.

examples.text: He *saw* his friends at the park yesterday.
examples.note: Indicates a past observation.

examples.text: We *made* a cake for the party.
examples.note: Refers to an action completed in the past.

examples.text: I had some engine trouble yesterday.
"When did you buy it?" "Let's see. I bought it last week."

commonErrors.note: The past simple of 'go' is 'went', not 'goed'.
The past simple of 'eat' is 'ate', not 'eated'.
Use the base form of the verb after 'did' or 'didn't'.

grammarPoints.title: Past simple: regular verbs
grammarPoints.summary: Use the past simple to talk about finished actions in the past with regular verbs, using '-ed' endings and 'did' for questions and negatives.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use the *past simple* to talk about actions that started and finished at a specific time in the past. This tense tells us that an action is completely over.

For most regular verbs, we form the past simple by adding *-ed* to the base form of the verb. For example, 'walk' becomes 'walked', and 'start' becomes 'started'.

To make questions and negative sentences in the past simple, we use the auxiliary verb *did*. For questions, we say 'Did + subject + base verb?'. For negatives, we say 'Subject + did not (didn't) + base verb'. Remember, when you use 'did' or 'didn't', the main verb always goes back to its base form.

examples.text: I *walked* to the store this morning.
examples.note: Describes a finished action in the past.

examples.text: She *studied* for her test last night.
examples.note: Shows a completed action using the -ed ending.

examples.text: They *didn't like* the movie.
examples.note: A negative sentence using 'didn't' and the base form of the verb.

examples.text: *Did* you *finish* your work?
examples.note: A question using 'Did' and the base form of the verb.

examples.text: We *played* board games all evening.
examples.note: Another example of a finished action with a regular -ed verb.

examples.text: It happened that he was out.
At first, I didn't like him.

commonErrors.wrong: I did walked to the park.
commonErrors.note: Do not use 'did' in affirmative past simple sentences with regular verbs.
After 'didn't', use the base form of the verb.
After 'Did' in a question, use the base form of the verb.

grammarPoints.title: Possessive 's
grammarPoints.summary: Use 's or ' to show that something belongs to someone or something.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use an apostrophe and 's' (*'s*) to show possession for *singular* nouns. This means that one person or thing owns something. For example, "David's car" means the car belongs to David.

For *plural* nouns that end in 's', we just add an apostrophe after the 's' (*s'*). For example, "the students' books" means the books belong to many students. If a plural noun does *not* end in 's' (like "children" or "people"), we add *'s* just like with singular nouns. For example, "the children's toys."

Possessive 's helps us make sentences shorter and clearer. Instead of saying "the bag of my friend," we can say "my friend's bag."

examples.text: My sister's name is Elena.
examples.note: Shows that the name belongs to one sister.

examples.text: The students' project is due tomorrow.
examples.note: Shows that the project belongs to many students (plural noun ending in 's').

examples.text: The children's playground is very big.
examples.note: Shows that the playground belongs to many children (irregular plural noun).

examples.text: Is this your friend's phone?
examples.note: Asks if the phone belongs to one friend.

examples.text: The cats' toys were all over the floor.
examples.note: Shows that the toys belong to multiple cats (plural noun ending in 's').

commonErrors.note: For plural possessive, the apostrophe comes after the 's'.
For singular possessive, add 's.
For irregular plural nouns, add 's.

grammarPoints.title: At, on and in for time
grammarPoints.summary: Learn to use 'at' for specific times, 'on' for days and dates, and 'in' for months, seasons, and years.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use *at* for very specific times. This includes clock times like 'at 7 PM' or 'at noon'. Think of it as a precise point in time.

We use *on* for days of the week and specific dates. For example, 'on Monday' or 'on July 4th'. If you can put 'day' after it, you probably use 'on'.

We use *in* for longer periods of time. This includes months ('in August'), seasons ('in summer'), and years ('in 2023'). We also use 'in' for parts of the day like 'in the morning' or 'in the evening'.
patterns: at + specific time (e.g., at 8 AM, at noon)
on + day of the week (e.g., on Tuesday, on Friday)
on + specific date (e.g., on May 1st, on Christmas Day)
in + month (e.g., in January, in October)
in + season/year/part of day (e.g., in summer, in 2025, in the morning)

examples.text: The store opens at 9 AM every day.
examples.note: Uses 'at' for a specific clock time.

examples.text: I have a meeting on Wednesday.
examples.note: Uses 'on' for a day of the week.

examples.text: Her birthday is in September.
examples.note: Uses 'in' for a month.

examples.text: We usually go on vacation in the summer.
examples.note: Uses 'in' for a season.

examples.text: The new building was finished in 2024.
examples.note: Uses 'in' for a year.

examples.text: We often play cards on Sunday.
Tom will be thirty in March.

commonErrors.note: Use 'at' for specific clock times.

commonErrors.wrong: I will call you at Friday.
commonErrors.right: I will call you on Friday.
commonErrors.note: Use 'on' for days of the week.
Use 'in' for months.

grammarPoints.title: Present continuous for arrangements
grammarPoints.summary: Use the present continuous to talk about future plans that are already arranged, often with a specific time or place.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use the *present continuous* to talk about future plans that are already decided and arranged. These are not just ideas, but plans that have a specific time, date, or place.

Think of it like looking at your calendar or schedule. If you have an appointment or a meeting written down, you can use the present continuous to talk about it.

It's common to use time expressions like "tomorrow," "next week," "on Friday," or "at 7 PM" with this grammar point to make it clear you are talking about the future.

examples.text: I'm meeting my sister for lunch tomorrow.
examples.note: This is a fixed arrangement for a specific time.

grammarPoints.title: Present perfect for experience
grammarPoints.summary: Use the present perfect to talk about experiences you've had (or haven't had) at any time in your life, without saying exactly when.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use the *present perfect* to talk about experiences that happened at some point in your life, but we don't say *when* exactly. It connects a past action to the present moment because the experience is still part of your life.

To form the present perfect, we use *have* or *has* followed by the *past participle* of the main verb. For example, "I *have visited* Paris." or "She *has tried* sushi."

We often use *ever* in questions to ask if someone has had an experience: "Have you *ever* eaten durian?" And we use *never* to say we haven't had an experience: "I've *never* seen snow."

examples.text: I have traveled to many different countries.
examples.note: Talking about general life experience.

examples.note: Stating an experience she hasn't had.

examples.text: Have you ever seen a shooting star?
examples.note: Asking about a past experience at any time.

examples.text: My brother has learned to play the guitar.
examples.note: An experience that happened in the past and is still relevant.

examples.text: We have visited that museum twice.
examples.note: An experience that happened in the past, without a specific time.

examples.text: Have you ever seen it?
Have you ever been here before?

commonErrors.note: Use present perfect with 'never' for life experiences.

grammarPoints.title: Just, already and yet
grammarPoints.summary: Learn to use 'just,' 'already,' and 'yet' with the present perfect to talk about recent actions and news.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use the present perfect with *just*, *already*, and *yet* to talk about things that happened a short time ago, or to ask if something has happened up to now.

*Just* means 'a very short time ago.' It tells us that an action happened very recently. We put *just* between 'have/has' and the past participle.

*Already* means 'before now' or 'sooner than expected.' It shows that an action has happened. We also put *already* between 'have/has' and the past participle.

*Yet* means 'up to now.' We use *yet* in questions and negative sentences. It usually goes at the end of the sentence.
patterns: Subject + have/has + not + past participle + yet

examples.text: I've just seen the new movie trailer.
examples.note: Shows the action happened a very short time ago.

examples.text: They have already finished their lunch.
examples.note: Indicates the action happened before now, perhaps sooner than expected.

commonErrors.note: Remember to use 'have' or 'has' with 'just' for recent actions.

commonErrors.note: 'Yet' usually goes at the end of negative sentences.

grammarPoints.title: Should for advice
grammarPoints.summary: Learn how to use 'should' to give and ask for advice or to make recommendations in English.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use the modal verb *should* to give advice or to say what we think is a good idea. It's a suggestion, not a strong obligation. For example, "You should try this new cafe." means it's a good idea to try it.

To give negative advice, we use *shouldn't* (should not). This means we think something is not a good idea. For instance, "You shouldn't eat too much sugar." is a recommendation to avoid it.

To ask for advice, we put *should* before the subject. For example, "Should I wear a jacket?" means you are asking for a recommendation about clothing.

grammarPoints.title: Some and any
grammarPoints.summary: Use 'some' for positive statements and offers, and 'any' for negative statements and questions.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use *some* in positive sentences with plural countable nouns (like 'apples', 'friends') and uncountable nouns (like 'water', 'money'). It means "an unspecified amount or number."

We also use *some* when we offer something or make a request, especially when we expect a positive answer.

We use *any* in negative sentences with plural countable nouns and uncountable nouns. It means "not even one" or "not an amount."

We also use *any* in most questions.

grammarPoints.title: Superlative adjectives
grammarPoints.summary: Use superlative adjectives to say something is the highest, lowest, or most extreme in a group of three or more.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use superlative adjectives to compare three or more things and say which one has the most or least of a quality. For most short adjectives (one or two syllables), we add *-est* to the end of the adjective. Remember to use *the* before the superlative adjective.

For longer adjectives (three or more syllables), we use *the most* before the adjective. We do not change the adjective itself.

Some common adjectives have irregular superlative forms. The superlative of 'good' is *the best*, and the superlative of 'bad' is *the worst*. Always use *the* with these forms too.

examples.text: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.

examples.text: This is the smallest phone I've ever seen.

examples.text: That movie was the most interesting one this year.

examples.text: She makes the best cookies in the neighborhood.
examples.note: Uses the irregular superlative 'best' to show her cookies are superior to all others.

examples.text: The traffic today is the worst I've experienced.
examples.note: Uses the irregular superlative 'worst' to describe the lowest quality of traffic.

examples.text: Of all the places I've been, Alaska is the most beautiful.

commonErrors.note: Always use 'the' before a superlative adjective.

grammarPoints.title: Too and enough
grammarPoints.summary: Use 'too' to say something is more than needed, and 'enough' to say there is the right amount or not enough.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use *too* to mean 'more than necessary' or 'more than wanted'. It shows that something is excessive. For example, if a shirt is "too small," it means it's smaller than you need or want.

We use *enough* to mean 'the right amount' or 'sufficient'. It shows that something is the correct amount or degree. If a room is "big enough," it means it has the size you need.

'Too' comes *before* an adjective or an adverb. 'Enough' comes *after* an adjective or an adverb. We also use 'enough' *before* a noun to talk about quantity. For example, "enough time" or "not enough money."

examples.text: The music is too loud.
examples.note: The volume is more than necessary or comfortable.

examples.text: He drives too fast on this road.
examples.note: His speed is excessive or dangerous.

examples.text: This jacket isn't warm enough for winter.

examples.text: Do we have enough food for all the guests?

examples.text: The car is too expensive for me to buy.
He has enough money to buy it.

commonErrors.note: 'Enough' comes before a noun.
'Enough' comes after an adjective.

commonErrors.wrong: It's very cold to go outside.
commonErrors.note: Use 'too' to show something is excessive, not just 'very'.

grammarPoints.title: Will for predictions and decisions
grammarPoints.summary: Use 'will' to talk about future predictions, offers, and decisions you make at the moment of speaking.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use *will* to talk about the future in several situations. One common use is for *predictions* – things we think will happen, but we are not 100% sure. For example, "I think it will rain tomorrow."

We also use *will* for *decisions made at the moment of speaking*. These are not plans you made before, but choices you make right now. For instance, if someone asks, "What would you like to drink?" you might say, "I'll have some water, please."

Finally, *will* is used for *offers* to help someone. If you see a friend struggling with heavy bags, you can say, "I'll help you with those." The negative form is *will not* or *won't*.

examples.text: I think the train will be late today.
examples.note: This is a prediction about the future.

examples.text: Oh, the phone is ringing. I'll answer it!
examples.note: This is a decision made at the moment of speaking.

examples.text: Don't worry, I'll help you carry those boxes.
examples.note: This is an offer to help someone.

examples.text: They won't finish the project by Friday.
examples.note: This is a negative prediction.

examples.text: Will you come to the concert with us?
examples.note: This is a question asking about a future action.

examples.text: It will stop raining soon.
I will find you a good doctor.

commonErrors.right: I think it will rain tomorrow.
commonErrors.note: Remember to use 'will' for future predictions.
Use 'won't' or 'will not' for negative future statements.

commonErrors.wrong: He will goes to the store.
commonErrors.right: He will go to the store.
commonErrors.note: After 'will', always use the base form of the verb.

grammarPoints.title: Would like and want
grammarPoints.summary: Learn to use 'would like' to politely express wishes for things or actions, and to make polite offers.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use *would like* to express a polite wish or desire. It is much more polite and softer than simply using *want*. For example, if you are in a restaurant, saying "I would like a glass of water" is more polite than "I want a glass of water."

We also use *would like* to make polite offers. For example, "Would you like some tea?" is a common way to offer a drink.

When you want to talk about an action, you use *would like to* followed by the base form of the verb. For example, "I would like to travel next year." or "Would you like to join us?"
patterns: Subject + would like to + verb (base form)
Would you like to + verb (base form)?

examples.text: I would like a new book for my birthday.
examples.note: Expresses a polite wish for a thing.

examples.text: Would you like some more cake?
examples.note: Makes a polite offer of a thing.

examples.text: My sister would like to learn to play the guitar.
examples.note: Expresses a polite wish for an action.

examples.text: Would you like to go to the park this afternoon?
examples.note: Makes a polite offer for an action.

examples.text: They would like to order pizza for dinner.
examples.note: Expresses a polite wish for an action.

examples.text: Would you like to eat lunch together?

commonErrors.note: Use 'would like' for polite requests, especially in formal situations.

commonErrors.wrong: She would like go to the beach.

commonErrors.note: Use the base form of the verb after 'would like to'.
